title: The verse you kept
tomorrow: Dadi says Amira has changed. should you count your own progress?

lines: A PRAYER THAT ASKS FOR NOTHING IN PARTICULAR.
cards: A surgery waiting room: a TV nobody watches, a vending machine humming, a screen of patient numbers turning from yellow to green. The surgery is running long.
Someone in the corner wants to pray, and doesn't know what to ask for. The knee? No pain?
Going home by Friday? Every request feels too small or too big. Back on day two hundred thirty, this path asked you to choose a verse to keep.
Here's one worth keeping for exactly this room, and it has a strange detail in it: a man at the end of his rope prays, and asks for nothing in particular.

teach.h: MUSA AT THE WELL IN MIDIAN.
teach.b: The man is Musa. He has fled Egypt with nothing and walked all the way to Midian. At a well, shepherds crowd in to water their flocks, and two women hold theirs back, waiting.
He waters their flock for them.
Then the Qur'an says he turned aside into the shade, and said: "My Lord! I am needy of whatever good thou sendest down for me." That's it. No food, no roof, no job, no name for what he wants.
Here's the puzzle: why such an open prayer from a man who needs everything? Look at the word. Faqir: needy, poor, empty-handed.
He names exactly where he stands, and leaves the shape of the answer to God. Whatever good.
And here's the detail to tell a friend tonight: the very next verse begins with one of the two women walking back to him shyly, bringing her father's invitation. A meal. Then work.
Then, later in the story, a marriage and a home. He never asked for any of it by name. That's what a kept verse is for.

teach.h: SHORT ENOUGH FOR A WAITING ROOM.
teach.b: Not a quotation to admire, but a line short enough to fit in a waiting room, when the long prayers won't come.
Musa's has three parts you can hold in one breath: My Lord. I am in need. Whatever good You send.

how: Many Muslims keep a favorite verse close, on a card, a phone screen or a framed print at home, and recite it in hard moments; Musa's prayer in 28:24 is one people often say when they need help and don't know what to ask.

games.q: what does “the verse you kept” mean?
o: a line of scripture you chose and carry
the first verse you were taught as a child
a verse you must recite in every prayer

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: the well where he helped two women
she walks back with an invitation

s: in the story, Musa asks God for food and a home by name
he says only: I am needy of whatever good Thou sendest down for me (28:24).
right after his prayer, one of the women comes back with her father's invitation

games.q: a friend got laid off and keeps rewriting a prayer list: the exact job, salary and city she wants. what might Musa's verse add?
o: keep the list tight; open-ended prayers don't really get answered.
name the need honestly, and leave room for whatever good comes.
stop asking at all, since asking shows a lack of trust.
games.why: Musa named exactly where he stood, needy, and asked for 'whatever good'. what came was more than he'd have known to list.

practice: Write your kept verse by hand, from memory if you can, on any scrap of paper. If none comes to mind, write Musa's: My Lord, I am needy of whatever good You send down for me.
Then say it once, slowly, out loud or under your breath, and fold the paper small.

wordCard.voice: The verse you kept: one line of the Qur'an, chosen long ago, carried until a day needs it.

orig.note: Arabic: needy, poor; Musa's word for himself in 28:24.

carryVoice: Carry this: one verse, kept, folded small enough to fit any room you wait in. Eleven of fifteen.

sources.q: My Lord! I am needy of whatever good thou sendest down for me.

sources.ref: Qur'an 28:22-28 (Musa at the well of Midian; the invitation, the work, the marriage)
